 * sampled as a texture. [HeadlessPuppetBrowser] implements only the control plane and
 * [FieldUiBrowserTexture] implements both. The wire encoding is covered by `PuppetBrowserProtocolTest`.
 */

/** Current observable state of an offscreen Chromium tab. */
data class PuppetBrowserState(
    val url: String = "about:blank",
    val title: String = "",
    val loading: Boolean = false,
    val canGoBack: Boolean = false,
    val canGoForward: Boolean = false,
    val audible: Boolean = false,
    val focused: Boolean = false,
    val unresponsive: Boolean = false,
    val crashed: Boolean = false,
    val cursor: String = "default",
    val navigationGeneration: Long = 0,
)

/** One browser or protocol event. Payloads deliberately retain Electron/CDP fields verbatim. */
data class PuppetBrowserEvent(
    val sequence: Long,
    val name: String,
    val payload: JsonObject,
)

enum class BrowserJavascriptWorld { MAIN, ISOLATED }
enum class BrowserJavascriptReturnMode { VALUE, HANDLE }

/** A JavaScript result, either copied by value or retained in Chromium as [objectId]. */
data class BrowserJavascriptResult(
    val type: String,
    val value: JsonElement = JsonNull,
    val description: String? = null,
    val unserializableValue: String? = null,
    val objectId: String? = null,
)

class PuppetBrowserCommandException(
    message: String,
    val command: String? = null,
    val details: JsonObject? = null,
) : RuntimeException(message)

enum class BrowserModifier(val cdpBit: Int) {
    ALT(1),
    CONTROL(2),
    META(4),
    SHIFT(8),
}

enum class BrowserMouseButton(val cdpName: String, val cdpBit: Int) {
    NONE("none", 0),
    LEFT("left", 1),
    RIGHT("right", 2),
    MIDDLE("middle", 4),
    BACK("back", 8),
    FORWARD("forward", 16),
}

enum class BrowserPointerType(val cdpName: String) { MOUSE("mouse"), PEN("pen") }
enum class BrowserPointerEventType { MOVE, DOWN, UP, WHEEL }

/** Browser pointer coordinates are CSS pixels, origin at the viewport's top-left. */
data class BrowserPointerEvent(
    val type: BrowserPointerEventType,
    val x: Double,
    val y: Double,
    val button: BrowserMouseButton = BrowserMouseButton.NONE,
    val buttons: Int = 0,
    val modifiers: Set<BrowserModifier> = emptySet(),
    val clickCount: Int = 0,
    val deltaX: Double = 0.0,

    val tiltY: Double = 0.0,

    val type: BrowserKeyEventType,
    val key: String,
    val code: String = key,
    val modifiers: Set<BrowserModifier> = emptySet(),

    val nativeVirtualKeyCode: Int = windowsVirtualKeyCode,
    val autoRepeat: Boolean = false,
    val keypad: Boolean = false,

    fun goBack(): CompletableFuture<PuppetBrowserState>
    fun goForward(): CompletableFuture<PuppetBrowserState>

    fun stop(): CompletableFuture<PuppetBrowserState>
    fun focus(): CompletableFuture<PuppetBrowserState>
    fun blur(): CompletableFuture<PuppetBrowserState>

    fun key(event: BrowserKeyEvent)
    fun insertText(text: String)
    fun setComposition(
        text: String,
        selectionStart: Int = text.length,
        selectionEnd: Int = selectionStart,
        replacementStart: Int? = null,

    put("y", y)
    put("button", button.cdpName)
    put("buttons", buttons)
    put("modifiers", modifiers.cdpBits())
    put("clickCount", clickCount)
    put("pointerType", pointerType.cdpName)
    put("force", pressure)
    put("tiltX", tiltX)
    put("tiltY", tiltY)
    put("twist", twist)

        put("deltaX", deltaX)
        put("deltaY", deltaY)

    put("type", type.cdpName)
    put("key", key)
    put("code", code)
    put("modifiers", modifiers.cdpBits())
    put("windowsVirtualKeyCode", windowsVirtualKeyCode)
    put("nativeVirtualKeyCode", nativeVirtualKeyCode)
    put("autoRepeat", autoRepeat)
    put("isKeypad", keypad)
    text?.let { put("text", it) }
    unmodifiedText?.let { put("unmodifiedText", it) }

internal fun touchToCdpJson(
    type: BrowserTouchEventType,
    points: List<BrowserTouchPoint>,
    modifiers: Set<BrowserModifier>,
): JsonObject = buildJsonObject {
    put("type", type.cdpName)
    put("modifiers", modifiers.cdpBits())
    put("touchPoints", buildJsonArray {
        points.forEach { point ->
            add(buildJsonObject {
                put("id", point.id)
                put("x", point.x)
                put("y", point.y)
                put("radiusX", point.radiusX)
                put("radiusY", point.radiusY)

internal fun puppetBrowserState(json: JsonObject): PuppetBrowserState = PuppetBrowserState(
    url = json.stringOrNull("url") ?: "about:blank",
    title = json.stringOrNull("title") ?: "",
    loading = json.boolean("loading"),
    canGoBack = json.boolean("canGoBack"),
    canGoForward = json.boolean("canGoForward"),
    audible = json.boolean("audible"),
    focused = json.boolean("focused"),
    unresponsive = json.boolean("unresponsive"),
    crashed = json.boolean("crashed"),
    cursor = json.stringOrNull("cursor") ?: "default",
    navigationGeneration = json["navigationGeneration"]?.jsonPrimitive?.longOrNull ?: 0,
)

internal fun browserJavascriptResult(json: JsonObject): BrowserJavascriptResult = BrowserJavascriptResult(
    type = json.stringOrNull("type") ?: "undefined",
    value = json["value"] ?: JsonNull,
    description = json.stringOrNull("description"),
    unserializableValue = json.stringOrNull("unserializableValue"),
    objectId = json.stringOrNull("objectId"),
)

internal fun JsonObject.objectOrNull(name: String): JsonObject? = this[name]?.let {
    if (it is JsonObject) it else null
}

internal fun JsonObject.stringOrNull(name: String): String? =
    this[name]?.jsonPrimitive?.contentOrNull

internal fun JsonObject.boolean(name: String): Boolean =
    this[name]?.jsonPrimitive?.booleanOrNull ?: false

# Depth and CLIP: neural vision in a box `afield.ai.inference.onnx` binds two pretrained vision models. Depth Anything V2 Small reads one photograph and predicts how far away everything in it is; CLIP embeds images and text into a shared 512-dimensional space, so a picture can be scored against a written prompt with no training and no label set. Both run on the ONNX Runtime JNI artifact (`com.microsoft.onnxruntime:onnxruntime`, 1.27.0), which is on the classpath already because [semantic search](semantic_index.md) embeds text with it. The weights are not: each model is fetched the first time you ask for it, and that is the whole install. The [`onnx_webcam_live`](agent_transcripts.md#onnx_webcam_live) starting point runs both models on a webcam frame in one box. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/onnx/overview.png" wait="30" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"} :::static import afield.ai.inference.onnx.* import java.nio.ByteBuffer import java.nio.ByteOrder :::fold load a photograph that ships with Field, and pack it as the RGBA8 bytes both models read val photo = imgFromFile("public/docs/assets/vision/fline-viewer.jpg", 3).scaleBy(0.45) fun toRgba8(img: Img): ByteBuffer { val out = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(img.width * img.height * 4).order(ByteOrder.nativeOrder()) for (p in 0 until img.pixelCount) { for (c in 0 until 3) { val v = (img.data[p * img.channels + c].coerceIn(0f, 1f) * 255f + 0.5f).toInt() out.put(p * 4 + c, v.toByte()) } out.put(p * 4 + 3, 255.toByte()) } return out } val rgbaBytes = toRgba8(photo) :::endfold // How far away is everything? — one image in, one single-channel map out. val depth = DepthAnything.forSource(photo.width, photo.height) depth.infer(rgbaBytes, photo.width, photo.height) depth.depthFp16 // ready to upload as VK_FORMAT_R16_SFLOAT // What is this a picture of? — no training, no labels, just prompts. val prompts = ClipText.encodeAll(["an empty room", "a person at a desk"]) val best = ClipImage().encode(rgbaBytes, photo.width, photo.height).best(prompts)!! // the better-matching label, and its share :::fold show both answers val depthMap = Img(depth.width, depth.height, 1, FloatArray(depth.width * depth.height) { depth.depthRaw.get(it) }) showImgGrid( "CLIP: \"%s\" (%.0f%%)".format(best.first, best.second * 100) to photo, "depth, bright = near" to depthMap.colormap("inferno").resize(photo.width, photo.height), columns = 2, cellSide = 500, ) :::endfold ``` ![](assets/onnx/overview.png) ## Sessions are cached, so a box can re-run Session construction is the *expensive* half of ONNX: the graph is parsed, fused and specialised for the execution provider, which costs hundreds of milliseconds. Inference is the cheap half. A box that says `DepthAnything(...)` and gets re-evaluated on every keystroke must not pay that on every keystroke. So `OnnxRuntime` keeps its sessions for the life of Field, outside any box. Re-running a box finds the session it built last time. [`FaustEngine`](faust.md#what-it-costs) does the same for compiled DSP. The first line below asks the cache; the second builds a session directly, and pays the full cost on every run: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} // Cached. # ORCA

[ORCA](https://github.com/hundredrabbits/Orca) is Hundred Rabbits' livecoding sequencer: a grid of
letters where every letter is an operator, every operator runs once a frame, and a `*` passing
next to one sets it off. `orca()` puts ORCA in a box's output. You type into it exactly as you
would into ORCA, and whatever it would send to a synthesizer arrives in your Kotlin instead.

This box plays a melody and a bass line through one of Field's small built-in synthesizers, and
shows the last note it heard:

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/orca/hello.png" alt="A Field box with two outputs. The orca output is ORCA's black grid: a comment reading ORCA IN FIELD, a clock C8 feeding a track operator T that holds the notes CDEGAGED, two MIDI operators lit in teal under a pair of delays, and ORCA's status lines along the bottom. Below it, the heard output reads the note, channel and MIDI number of the last note Kotlin received." capture="box" open-outputs="true" wait-output=true wait-output-kind=display wait-output-channel="heard" wait="3" timeout="180" embed=true name="orca-hello" w="760" h="560" padding="18"}
val synth = PatSynthBank()
val o =
    orca(
        rows = 12,
        grid =
            """
    #.ORCA.IN.FIELD.#
    .
    .2C8
    D2.8TCDEGAGED
    .:04
    .
    D8
    .:12C
""",
    )
o.onNote {
    synth.play(it)
    markdown("heard", "`${it.note}${it.octave}` on channel ${it.channel}, MIDI ${it.midi}")
}
displayOpen("heard")
synth
```

Returning `synth` from the box is what makes it sound: [PatSynthBank](sound_paths.md) plays through
Field's audio engine for as long as the box runs. Stop the box and ORCA stops with it. This is
eight seconds of it:

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin audio="assets/orca/hello.wav" audio-spec="hello" audio-renderer="afield.audio.synth.OrcaSoundDocs" embed=true hidden=true name="orca-hello-audio"}
// OrcaSoundDocs.render("hello"): the grid above, run by ORCA's own operators, voiced by PatSynthBank
```

[Open the ORCA starting point ↗](offline.html?file=assets/agent_transcripts/orca_hello/metadata.edn)
to have this box in a document of your own.

Click the grid to give ORCA the keyboard: arrows move, letters write, **Space** plays and pauses,
**Escape** puts the cursor back, **ctrl/command-K** opens ORCA's command line, and **ctrl/command-G** shows its guide
to every operator. [ORCA's README](https://github.com/hundredrabbits/Orca#operators) lists the
operators too.

## What comes back

Each operator that talks to the outside world has a callback. They run once per frame, in the
order ORCA played them, with the box in context, so they can `display`, `print` and change box state.

| ORCA | Kotlin | you get |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `:` MIDI note | `onNote { }` | `OrcaNote`: `channel`, `octave`, `note` as ORCA writes it, `midi`, `hz`, `velocity` (0 to 1), `frames` and `seconds` long |
| `%` mono note | `onNote { }` | the same, with `mono` true |
| `!` control change | `onCC { }` | `OrcaCC`: `channel`, `knob`, `value` (0 to 127) |
| `?` pitch bend | `onBend { }` | `OrcaBend`: `channel`, `lsb`, `msb` |
| `;` UDP | `onUdp { }` | the text after the `;` |
| `=` OSC | `onOsc { }` | `OrcaOsc`: `path`, and `args` as the values of the glyphs after it |
| any cell changing | `onChange { }`, `onCell(x, y) { }` | `OrcaCell`: `x`, `y`, `before`, `after`; or the new glyph |
| every frame | `onFrame { }` | the `Orca`: `grid`, `frame`, `bpm`, `playing`, `variables`, `cursor` |

ORCA's MIDI output still goes to a MIDI device if the browser has one, as it does in ORCA itself.

## Writing to it

`write(x, y, text)` puts glyphs on the grid with their top
left at `(x, y)`; a newline in `text` starts the next row back at `x`. Setting `grid` replaces the
whole thing. `command(...)` runs anything ORCA's command line takes, and `play()`, `stop()` and
`bpm` are there by name. Added to the first example, these three lines speed it up, put a third
voice under it, and pick a new melody each time the bass plays:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
o.bpm = 140
o.write(0, 9, "D4\n.:03C")
o.onNote { if (it.channel == 1) o.write(5, 3, ["CDEGAGED", "EGBDBGEB"].random()) }
```

A change reaches ORCA at its next frame. Inside a coroutine, `o.sync()` waits until ORCA has applied everything sent so far and
reported back, so `o.grid` shows the result.

A box can also work cell by cell, as one more operator. `o[x, y]` reads a glyph and

## Pixels without readback

The browser and renderer stay separate processes. Chromium produces an accelerated offscreen paint
with a native GPU handle and an explicit lease. Field imports that image, performs one GPU copy into
a stable resident `VkImage`, and returns the lease only after the graphics fence says the copy has
finished. The path stays on the GPU throughout: **Chromium compositor** → native shared texture and
lease → platform import → stable resident Vulkan image → **any Field mesh, shader, render target
or OpenXR panel**.

The copy exists so that Chromium can reuse its buffer; it happens on the GPU. No screenshot,
encoded frame or pixel array travels between Electron and the shader. The resident image is imported as sRGB, so ordinary page
colour survives the trip into the renderer correctly.

On macOS the transferred object is an IOSurface sent through a Mach port. MoltenVK backs a Vulkan
image with it; KosmicKrisp, the default driver on recent Apple silicon, maps its pages as a buffer
and copies them into an image on the GPU. On Windows and Linux the GPU transfer is refused with a
message, and `cpuBitmapFallback = true` reads frames back instead.

a desktop or exposing an Electron window.

| Surface | What is available |
| --- | --- |
| State | URL, title, loading, history availability, audio, focus, cursor, responsiveness, crash state and navigation generation |
| Navigation | Navigate, back, forward, reload with or without cache, stop, focus and blur |
| Pointer | Move, five mouse buttons, wheel, click count, modifiers, mouse or pen pressure, tilt and twist |
| Text input | Raw key down/up, repeat, physical key codes, Unicode text insertion and IME composition |
| Touch | Multi-point start, move, end and cancel events with radius, rotation and force |

The fire-and-forget input calls preserve their order. `flushInput()` is a barrier when the next
operation must observe every earlier click or keystroke. Commands return `CompletableFuture`s, and
failures arrive as `PuppetBrowserCommandException` with the rejected command and Chromium details.

### JavaScript is a real request/response channel

Evaluation awaits returned promises. It can carry JSON-compatible values back to Kotlin, retain a
remote object in Chromium for later CDP work, or report the page's actual exception rather than
silently returning `undefined`:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
browserControl

    .evaluate(

        world = BrowserJavascriptWorld.ISOLATED,

`userGesture = true` matters for the same things it matters for in an ordinary browser: media
playback and APIs guarded by an active user gesture. The isolated world is useful for inspection or
instrumentation that should not add names to the page's own JavaScript environment.

`PuppetBrowser` extends `PuppetBrowserControl` and `ExternalBrowserSurface` together, so a box that

paint handler differs.

surface as an `ERR_ABORTED` against the new navigation.

only a picture it can show. The queries are extensions on `PuppetBrowserControl`, so they work
equally on a headless browser and on a `FieldUiBrowserTexture` already in your scene:

readings.column("station") // [alpha, beta, gamma]
readings.numbers("depth") // [12.0, 48.0, 93.0]

trip, and a condition that throws fails at once instead of being retried until the deadline.

wants: labels down one and values down another.

window ray, intersect its own geometry, and return whichever UV belongs under the pointer.

    if (event.name == "console" || event.name == "javascript-exception") println("${event.name}: ${event.payload}")
}

browserControl.cdp("Network.enable")
browserControl.cdp("Performance.enable")
browserControl.cdp("Performance.getMetrics").thenAccept { println(it) }

browserControl.forwardCdpEvents(true)
```

The named listener replaces its predecessor on this browser; Stop or rerun of the registering
box removes it.

The normal event stream already includes state changes, navigation, load failures, page titles,
console messages, cursor changes, context menus, audio state, pop-up attempts, permission requests,
JavaScript dialogs and exceptions, responsiveness and renderer exits. Turning on CDP forwarding
adds protocol events as `cdp` messages for tools that want Network, Runtime, Debugger, Performance
or any other domain. So Field can build the diagnostics it wants without recreating the visual
DevTools shell in VR.

### A sandboxed page can call back into Field

The preload exposes only two JSON-cloning operations—`window.fieldPuppet.emit` and
`window.fieldPuppet.request`—rather than Node or an unrestricted IPC object. Field chooses the
request names it will accept:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val removeBridge =
    browserControl.onPageRequest("selected-point") { payload ->
        println("page selected $payload")
        CompletableFuture.completedFuture(
            buildJsonObject { put("accepted", true) },
        )
    }
requireNotNull(RunScope.current()).own { removeBridge() }
```

```diffstatic {data-lang=javascript}
const answer = await window.fieldPuppet.request("selected-point", {
    x: event.clientX,
    y: event.clientY
})
```

This is enough for a cooperative application to expose semantic actions while the generic pointer,
keyboard and CDP paths remain available for every other site.

## A browser you do not have to render

Everything in the table above is about the *tab*, not about its pixels, and none of it needs a
Vulkan image view, a window or a GPU.
`PuppetBrowserControl`, in the same file, is the control plane on its own, and
`HeadlessPuppetBrowser` (`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/media/browser/HeadlessPuppetBrowser.kt`)
implements it with no renderer, no Vulkan surface, no native handle bridge and no readback socket.
The Electron producer has a third frame mode in which the paints are dropped at the source.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val browser = HeadlessPuppetBrowser("https://field.graphics/")
try {
    browser.loaded.get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    println("${browser.state.title} at ${browser.state.url}")
} finally {
    browser.close()
}
```

`PuppetBrowser` extends `PuppetBrowserControl` and `ExternalBrowserSurface` together, so a box that
publishes `browserControl` publishes the control plane whether or not anything is drawing it, and
every example on this page reaches the same commands.

The producer, the wire protocol and every command are the ones the textured browser uses; only the
paint handler differs.

Constructing a browser with a URL and navigating in the very next statement is safe: `navigate`
waits for the producer's un-awaited first load to settle, so Chromium cancelling that load cannot
surface as an `ERR_ABORTED` against the new navigation.

### Pages as data

Once a page can be driven without being drawn, the web becomes a source Field can read rather than
only a picture it can show. The queries are extensions on `PuppetBrowserControl`, so they work
equally on a headless browser and on a `FieldUiBrowserTexture` already in your scene:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val readings = browser.table("#readings").get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)

readings.header // [station, depth, count]
readings.column("station") // [alpha, beta, gamma]
readings.numbers("depth") // [12.0, 48.0, 93.0]

browser.text("h1") // the first heading, or null
browser.texts("p.note") // every match, in document order
browser.attribute("#link", "href") // the markup's value, not the resolved URL
browser.count("#readings tbody tr") // 3
browser.waitFor("document.readyState === 'complete'")
```

These queries evaluate in an isolated world, so a page that has shadowed
`document.querySelectorAll` or shipped a polyfill cannot change what Field reads out of it.
`numbers` returns null, not zero, for a cell that is not a number, so a plot can tell a missing
reading from a reading of zero. `waitFor` waits in the page, so the whole wait costs one round
trip, and a condition that throws fails at once instead of being retried until the deadline.

`column` and `numbers` read a table's columns out side by side, which is what a Plotly or FLine box
wants: labels down one and values down another.

## How desktop events land on the page

`PuppetBrowserWindowInput` (`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/media/browser/PuppetBrowserInteraction.kt`)
turns Field window events into Chromium input:

1. the panel's aspect-correct viewport hit-tests the native cursor;
2. the hit becomes normalized panel UVs;
3. UVs become Chromium CSS pixels using the tab's device scale factor;
4. buttons are captured until release, even if the cursor leaves the panel;
5. key transitions keep their modifiers, scan codes, repeat and keypad identity; and
6. the character callback separately inserts Unicode text, while focus loss releases every held
   button and blurs the page.

The mapping is replaceable. A planar window uses a rectangle, but a curved screen can unproject a
window ray, intersect its own geometry, and return whichever UV belongs under the pointer.

## Then put the browser in VR

`PuppetBrowserVrPanel` places the same browser texture on a correctly proportioned world-space
quad. It is rendered once per eye, so the panel has actual stereo distance instead of being pasted
over the final headset image.

val stereo = SideBySideStereoTarget(renderer, openXR = renderer.openXRHmdTarget)
val panel = PuppetBrowserVrPanel(
    renderer = renderer,
    stereo = stereo,
    browser = browser,
    widthMeters = 1.6f,
    distanceMeters = 1.7f,
)
panel.build()
panel.enableDesktopInteraction()
```

The packed image above shows both eyes, as in the [ImGui VR panel](imgui_vr_panel.md): on a headset
the two views go to the eye swapchains; on a desktop they remain side by side as the development
preview. Each eye sees the same 1.6 m × 0.9 m browser panel from a slightly different position.

Each frame the interaction layer:

1. takes the OpenXR controller pose and projects its forward ray;
2. intersects that ray with the panel plane and converts the local hit to browser UVs;
3. maps select or trigger to a captured primary click;
4. maps the touched thumbstick or trackpad to page scrolling; and
5. leaves physical keyboard and IME input available for search boxes, editors and forms.

With no headset, Field's mouse-driven controller stand-in exercises the same ray, hit test, hover,
click and scroll path. The fragment shader draws a small ring at the browser UV currently under the
ray, so the preview also shows what Chromium is about to receive.

## The kaleidoscope: a whole tab as 224 triangles

Once the browser is an ordinary native texture, a rectangle is only a convention. This example opens
a YouTube watch page, handles the EU consent page, starts its real video element, and fractures the
complete tab into 224 animated triangles:

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin requires="browser-bridge,electron-runtime" screenshot="assets/puppet_browser/youtube-kaleidoscope.png" wait="12" timeout="90" capture="native-window" native-wait-frames="8" graphics-context=true embed=true name="youtube-kaleidoscope" alt="A live YouTube page fractured into 224 animated triangular Vulkan shards" macro-file="../../dev_docs/agents/transcripts/youtube_kaleidoscope.yaml" capture-box="youtube_kaleidoscope_renderer"}
val shards = PuppetBrowserKaleidoscope(
    renderer = renderer,
    browser = browser,
    columns = 14,
    rows = 8,
)
shards.motion = 1.0f
shards.facets = 5.0f
shards.chroma = 1.0f
shards.build()
```

`PuppetBrowserKaleidoscope` builds a 14 × 8 grid and cuts every cell diagonally. Duplicated vertices
let all 224 triangles move independently. The vertex stage opens moving cracks; the fragment stage
performs an aspect-correct polar fold, twist and zoom per shard, separates the RGB sample positions,
and uses barycentric distance for the narrow glass edge.

??? aside "How this figure is made"

    The figure comes from replaying `dev_docs/agents/transcripts/youtube_kaleidoscope.yaml`, which

    path is covered by `HeadlessPuppetBrowserTest`, which loads a committed `file://` fixture in a

WebGL can apply a kaleidoscope to a cooperative `<video>` element. Here the source is the
browser's fully composited tab (cross-origin video, consent UI, DOM, fonts, controls and later
navigations), and it enters an arbitrary native Vulkan/OpenXR pipeline without
canvas pixel access or cooperation from the page.
